title: A Last-Minute Diwali Party Menu for 6 to 8, Ready in About Two Hours
excerpt: Drinks, dips, chaat, hot starters, one hearty main and dessert — a six-course Diwali spread built on one shopping list and one timeline, using Slurrp's shelf-life rules to keep every dish at its best.
body:
• A complete Diwali spread for 6-8 guests can come together in about two hours if it is built in courses: drinks, dips, chaat, hot starters, one hearty main and desserts.
  • The working rule from Slurrp's Diwali menu planning is to cook by shelf life — long-life sweets and dry namkeen first, anything best crisp or best hot last.
  • Crisp items stay crisp only if they cool completely before being boxed airtight, with parchment between layers; dal gets its tadka just before serving.
  • For diaspora hosts, the two-hour format fits a weekday Diwali evening: one shopping list, one timeline, no dish that needs a day of prep.

Diwali falls on Sunday, November 8 this year, and for many households the party decision happens late. The good news is that a full festive spread does not need a full day in the kitchen. The last-minute format doing the rounds this season is a six-part menu for 6-8 guests — drinks, dips, chaat, hot starters, a hearty main course and desserts — designed to come together in about two hours, according to the menu plan published by Food Techniquez.

Build the menu in courses, not dishes

The structure is what makes two hours realistic. Drinks and dips go out the moment guests arrive, chaat is assembled to order rather than cooked, and only the hot starters and the main course need the stove at the same time. Desserts come from the sweets you already have in the house — no Diwali home is without mithai this week — which removes the most time-consuming course from the clock entirely.

What Slurrp's classic menu adds: shelf-life thinking

Slurrp's traditional Diwali menu for 2026 organises 15 classics — five sweets including besan ladoo and kaju katli, namkeen and snacks including chakli and dhokla, and mains built around dal — around one principle a last-minute host can steal: cook by shelf life. Long-life sweets and dry namkeen keep 5-10 days at room temperature in an airtight box, medium-life components can be prepped days ahead, and anything best hot or best crisp is finished last.

Three of Slurrp's storage notes matter even on a two-hour timeline. First, fried snacks such as chakli must cool completely before boxing — trapped heat softens the coil. Second, kaju katli should be wrapped tight and kept away from steam or heat so it does not sweat. Third, a dal cooked ahead should get its tadka — the tempered-spice finish — only just before serving, and steamed items such as dhokla are best the same day, tempered right before they go out.

A two-hour running order

Start with the counter, not the stove: clear space, set out containers and serving spoons, and box the sweets first so dessert is done before cooking begins. Put the main course on early because it reheats and holds well, assemble chaat components while it simmers, and fry or heat the hot starters last so they reach the table crisp. Drinks and dips go out as guests arrive, buying you the final half hour in the kitchen.

The diaspora version of this plan has one extra advantage: most of the menu travels well between homes and time zones of celebration. If you are hosting after work on a weekday evening in the US, the same order of operations applies — sweets bought or made on the weekend, one main cooked fresh, chaat assembled at the table, and nothing on the menu that punishes you for starting at 6 p.m.
